findings.reason: All four authentic original standalone tiles contain the full algebraic nested-interval proof but no figure. A one-step spatial picture materially clarifies the fixed-order rule: when u<y<s the first third contains y, while both subsequent thirds avoid it and the second must be retained. This is a warranted explanatory diagram under the expanded scope, not evidence of a gap in the proof.

diagram_math_checks.objects: At a fixed n, u=a_n<v=b_n, d=v-u, s=u+d/3 and t=s+d/3; y=f(n).
diagram_math_checks.check: Step 2.1 gives u<s<t<v with three equal positive lengths. Coordinates 0,3,6,9 represent precisely this order and equal trisection. y is shown at 1.5 only for the explicitly stated case u<y<s; no universal location of f(n) is asserted.

Because u<y<s, y belongs to [u,s]. Because y<s<t, it belongs to neither [s,t] nor [t,v]. The ordered list in step 2.1 therefore returns the second interval, not the third; step 5.1 identifies its endpoints with a_sigma(n), b_sigma(n). The lower segment spans exactly the same s,t coordinates, joined by vertical dashed endpoint identifiers.

diagram_math_checks.relation: x belongs to [s,t], and y does not.
diagram_math_checks.check: Steps 7.1 and 8.1 define x as the supremum of all left endpoints and place it in every retained closed interval, including index sigma(n). Thus x lies in this [s,t] whereas y=f(n) does not, as used in step 9.1. Closed dots denote inclusion of both endpoints. No dot places x in the strict interior; the caption explicitly allows endpoint membership.
